prize_parts.citation: for showing with credible causal evidence how import competition and technological change reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality

statement.case_for: B032 is my first choice after the opening round. The work combines a conceptual account of how tasks, technology and trade exposure shift labour demand with large-scale, transparent causal designs on local labour-market adjustment. It has changed how economists and policymakers think about who loses from structural change, and why adjustment is slow and uneven. That question is old in economic history, but this literature gave it a modern empirical footing. The main findings have been replicated, challenged and extended for over a decade, so the programme has been tested rather than merely cited. I have narrowed my proposed set from Autor, Hanson and Katz to Autor, Hanson and Dorn. The reason is that the most distinctive, best-identified and most clearly attributable body of work is the trade-shock research. Colleagues' openings show that crediting the broader task and skill-bias framework runs into names outside this ballot, and it overlaps with prior recognition of Goldin and Acemoglu. A citation anchored on the trade-shock papers, with the technology and tasks context in the wording, is the cleaner attribution.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the ballot item bundles two strands, the task and skill-demand framework and the China-shock empirics, and a three-name prize cannot credit both fairly. The task framework owes much to Acemoglu, Restrepo, Levy and Murnane, and Katz's skill-premium work, and some of that credit lies outside the proposed set. The magnitudes and persistence of the China-shock effects, and the shift-share identification behind them, are still debated. A committee that regards the contribution as a strong empirical programme on one episode rather than a general discovery could reasonably rank B010 or B019 higher.

responses.point: Hassler ranks the heterogeneous-firm trade work first. He argues it extends well beyond the earlier new-trade-theory prize, and that the framework has twenty-plus years of confirmation. He also observes that the B032 ballot item mixes the trade-shock work with the broader tasks agenda, which leaves open who should be credited.
responses.response: I agree with the B010 case on maturity and distinctness from 2008, and I treat B010 as my main alternative. On B032 his point about mixing strands persuaded me to change my laureate set. I dropped Katz, who anchors the long-run skills and technology framework, and now credit the trade-shock core of Autor, Dorn and Hanson, with the citation worded around trade and technology exposure. Where I still differ is on what matters most for the prize: B032's causal evidence on adjustment costs reaches labour, political and distributional questions beyond trade models, and its estimates have been stress-tested for a decade rather than only used as a framework.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B032 fourth. He values the transparent, well-identified designs and their policy salience. He is concerned that Katz's contributions partially overlap with the 2023 prize for Goldin, that the task framework has antecedents outside the list, and that the longer-run conclusions are still contested.
responses.response: I accept the overlap and antecedent concerns, and they are why Katz is no longer in my set. I would qualify the maturity worry. Debate about magnitudes and persistence is evidence that the findings have been scrutinised, not that they are fragile. The qualitative result, that regional adjustment to import shocks is slow and costly, has survived re-examination. I accept that the long-run aggregate welfare picture is unsettled, and a citation should not claim more than the evidence shows. That is why mine speaks of reshaping labour demand and local labour markets, not of settled welfare conclusions.

responses.point: Boppart ranks the collateral-constraint credit-cycles work (B019) first and proposes Kiyotaki and Moore as a clean two-person attribution. He treats Gertler and Gilchrist as an adjacent strand that overlaps with the 2022 recognition.
responses.response: I agree that the Kiyotaki-Moore attribution is cleaner than B032's, and that is a real advantage for B019. It is my fifth choice, mainly because direct empirical identification of the collateral channel is indirect, and because the 2022 prize covered the financial-crises theme. I would weigh clean credit against how convincingly the mechanism has been measured. B032 has the more direct causal evidence, though its attribution is messier. If the committee puts weight on credit clarity, B019 is the strongest macro alternative, but I would not put it ahead of the labour-market work.

responses.point: Krusell ranks the New Keynesian framework first, with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford as the foundational pricing, rule and normative-framework contributions. He accepts that a three-person limit omits important contributors.
responses.response: I rank B037 seventh, for the reason he concedes: the credit is diffuse across at least eight names. A three-person cut necessarily omits people with strong claims, such as Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets. My other concern is the post-2021 inflation episode, which reopened questions about the baseline model. His choice of Calvo, Taylor and Woodford is defensible, but I think it is less secure as a single prize unit than the B010 or B032 attributions.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the trade-shock strand or the broader task and skill-demand framework as the core of B032, which would change the laureate set, including whether Katz should replace Dorn.
How far the long-run persistence and magnitude of China-shock effects, and the shift-share identification behind them, will hold up under continued re-examination.
How the committee weighs B032 against B010, which has far broader opening support and a cleaner two-name attribution, and against B019, whose credit structure is cleaner.
The overlap of this work with recent recognition of Goldin (2023) and Acemoglu (2024), and whether it is judged a distinct advance.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. I have no documented connection to Autor, Hanson, Dorn, Katz or the other shortlisted candidates. My profile notes only Lund colleagues and economic-history co-authors, and my background in economic history and historical data work may incline me toward archival and measurement-heavy research. I note this as a possible bias, not as a conflict.
